On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is free and holds all the power: he commands Sitaram to open the door, draws his sword, and Sitaram—the subordinate guard—is helpless, pleading, refuses to resist only because Udayaditya once saved his life twice, and submits to being disarmed and bound by the prince. By the night of Udayaditya's own escape from prison, the roles are inverted: Udayaditya is now the imprisoned, helpless captive, while Sitaram is the free man with agency—he comes to the cell, directs the rescue amid the fire, grabs and nearly carries Udayaditya out, and answers his disoriented question of "What should I do? Where should I go?" by telling him to follow. Thus the master becomes the dependent, and the bound guard becomes the one in control.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray on the road—while he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his journey to Jessore. This plan failed because the Pathan left on the task (Khan Saheb) could not bring himself to slay the old, kind king and instead spared his life.

The method that finally succeeds is an execution ordered directly by Pratapaditya: Muktiyar Khan arrives at Raigarh bearing the Maharaja's signed death warrant for the King of Raigarh. After Basanta Ray completes his evening prayers and prostrates before his chosen deity, saying "Saheb, now!", Muktiyar calls in a soldier named Abdul, who enters with a drawn sword and beheads the old king—a stream of blood flowing in the room.

1. **In the inner quarters (the Mahishi's room, where the Mahishi was feeding the servants)** — disguised as a **middle-aged woman** (Ramai Thakur posing as "Mother Nikasha"). Here Rammohan tears the cloth from his head, lifts him into the air, swings him around, and ties him up with a shawl, slinging him over his shoulder out of the inner quarters.

2. **In the king's room (where the king and the jester Ramai Bhand were seated)** — in his plain guise as the **court jester**. Here Rammohan forcefully grabs Ramai by the scruff of his neck and throws him out of the room.

Surma does not go to her father's house at all; instead, she dies by taking poison. The covert action is that the Rajmahishi, with Pratapaditya's consent, secretly had Matangini procure poison (a medicine prepared with mantras and rituals by the widow Mangala, who knew tantra, mantra, and medicine), which Surma then consumed, causing her death.

Because Vibha refused to go the first time, Rammohan returned to Ramchandra Ray humiliated and dishonored before the king. Enraged by this perceived insult to his honor, the king resolved to take revenge and decided to marry another woman. Consequently, when Vibha finally arrives at Chandradwip, she learns that the king is getting married and has offered no forgiveness—her hopes of reuniting with her husband are shattered, and her entire world collapses at the very gates of the royal palace.

Rukmini (Mangala) tricked Udayaditya into giving her his ring during a stormy night when she entered his room and emotionally manipulated him, claiming he had ruined her; when she asked for "that ring on your finger," he pulled it off and threw it to her. The ring bore a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's name. Sitaram and Bhagavat then used this ring to stamp a forged petition—written to look as though Udayaditya was secretly lodging a treason complaint against Pratapaditya with the Emperor to seize the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat delivered this sealed, forged petition to Pratapaditya. When Pratapaditya saw the petition bearing his son's official seal, it served as the evidence of treason that prompted him to order Udayaditya's imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray's midnight escape set off a chain of events: after the escape, Pratapaditya dismissed the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat. Udayaditya, unable to bear their families going hungry, began giving the two dismissed men monthly stipends, which enraged Pratapaditya and prompted him to forbid any further financial help to them. When Udayaditya defied this, Surma took it upon herself to secretly send stipends to Sitaram's mother and Bhagavat's wife through a trusted maid. That secret arrangement (revealed through the maid to Mangala) reached Pratapaditya's ears, and in response he ordered that Surma be sent away to her paternal home—thus decreeing her exile.

**Emotional significance:** The song is the lament of total bereavement and isolation—of being the sole survivor of a once loving, joyful family. It voices the emptiness of having lost everyone ("what remains is only emptiness"), of having no one left to answer his call or to sing for, and the despair of going on living with only himself.

**Two contrasting contexts in which Basanta Ray sings it:**

1. **Alone, in wistful solitude (Chapter 27):** Sitting by himself on his palace veranda in Raigarh in the afternoon, gazing at the setting sun beyond the mango grove, he hums/sings it to himself. Here it rises spontaneously from a bittersweet mingling of lingering joy and longing for his loved ones—before he has learned the full extent of the tragedy—and its sorrow is underscored by his broken, untunable sitar.

2. **With Vibha, amid actual desolation (Chapter 28):** In the dark, empty household at Jessore, after seeing that only Vibha remains and that Surma's room is silent and utterly vacant, he takes Vibha's hand and slowly begins to sing it aloud—a shared, heart-rending lament confronting the reality of the family's destruction.

Because Rukmini failed to stop the escape, Udayaditya fled to Raigarh and remained under Basanta Ray's protection. Consumed by thwarted rage and thirst for revenge, Rukmini then went to Pratapaditya and revealed that the old king (Basanta Ray), Sitaram, and the Yubaraj had all conspired in the escape and the fire, declaring, "Give me men, and I will go myself and find them." She then led Pratapaditya's men to Raigarh, where she pointed out Udayaditya to Muktiyar Khan's soldiers. Having learned of Basanta Ray's involvement and located the fugitives, Pratapaditya issued a secret order—the death sentence for the King of Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan carried out that order, and Basanta Ray was beheaded. Thus, had Rukmini stopped the escape, none of this chain—her disclosure, the tracking to Raigarh, and the resulting execution order—would have unfolded.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra Ray coldly and dismissively—no proper welcome was sent out (the Dewanji only came to meet him after he had traveled two krosh past Chakdihi, with a modest retinue and a small elephant), and when they met, Pratapaditya showed "no slightest joy or haste," made Ramchandra stand while he attended to state business, ignored him, and finally dismissed him casually with "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters"—leaving Ramchandra to understand "in what way Pratapaditya was superior to him."

In parallel, Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya's status in his own court by constantly belittling and mocking him—asserting his own superiority. His courtiers fire "piercing verbal arrows" at Pratapaditya daily; the Dewan claims Pratapaditya's father had to beg Ramchandra's grandfather to anoint him (with the little toe of his foot); Ramai Bhand derides Pratapaditya's lineage as descended from an earthworm and leech; and the courtiers taunt that marrying into their family "is enough to redeem your seven generations" and that Ramchandra "stepped in the mud" by doing so.

In short, both treat the other as the inferior: Pratapaditya through a cold, neglectful, dismissive reception, and Ramchandra through retaliatory public mockery and denigration of Pratapaditya's rank and ancestry.

The widow Rukmini from Raigarh re-enters as "Mangala." After leaving Raigarh and changing her name, she settles on the outskirts of Jessore, where she uses her beauty and money (lending at interest) to control people. Driven by envy and a craving to rule both Udayaditya's heart and the kingdom of Jessore, she befriends all the palace servants to keep tabs on everything and performs tantric rituals hoping for the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma. Exploiting the growing hostility of the King and Rajmahishi toward Surma, she secretly prepares a poison (chanting mantras so the Yubaraj would feel no pity) and, through Matangini, supplies it to the Rajmahishi—leading to Surma taking poison and dying. She then personally reappears in Udayaditya's life, entering his bedchamber at night to demand his love and his ring.

Udayaditya's lifelong aversion to his birthright—expressed from the start in his wish that he had never been born a crown prince, that he had been tested as an heir rather than loved as a son, and his conviction that he lacked the intellect to rule (reinforced by the failure of the Hosenkhali pargana and his father's resulting contempt)—finally reaches its conclusion after a catastrophe that leaves him consumed with guilt over being a weakness that ruins everyone near him. On the journey to Jessore, reflecting that "those who were the joy of the world, the hope of the world—they were destroyed for my sake," he resolves, "No more, I am taking my leave of this world." Brought as a prisoner before Pratapaditya, he formally pleads, "I do not want your kingdom—grant me release from your throne." To prove it is genuine, he swears an oath touching the feet of Ma-Kali that he will never rule even "a needle's tip worth" of the land and that Samaraditya will be the heir. He then asks only not to be caged, requesting permission to leave for Kashi as an ascetic, where he will establish a guest house and a temple in his grand-uncle's name—thus transforming his childhood lament into a formal, sworn renunciation of the throne.

Nayanchand was entrusted with carrying Ramchandra Ray's spiteful letter (in which he declared he had renounced Vibha and asked that she not be sent to Chandradwip again) to Jessore, but, fearing what Pratapaditya might do if the letter fell into his hands, he did not deliver it and instead gave it to the Mahishi. The Mahishi, alarmed, kept it hidden from both Pratapaditya (telling him only a vague, hypothetical worry) and from Vibha (fearing it would destroy her). She then handed the letter to Basanta Ray. Interpreting it through his simple heart as mere anger that would pass once Vibha was sent back, Basanta Ray advised announcing throughout the household that Ramchandra had written requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip. Thus the letter's true meaning was reversed and misrepresented to Vibha as a request for her return, when in fact it had been a renunciation of her.
Rammohan and his followers physically pulled the boat up and over the large sal wood logs that Pratapaditya had ordered placed to block the canal, allowing the boat to escape past the obstruction.

Basanta Ray's sitar, described as his "eternal companion," is bound up with his joy and with the loved ones he plays for, so his estrangement from it mirrors his inner desolation over Udayaditya. In Chapter 13, even before departing, his grief disrupts his playing: he takes up the sitar and plays "furiously," but his blurring eyes and choked throat force him to stop and set it down, and his farewell words are, "I am leaving this sitar behind, Dada, I will not play it anymore." In Chapter 27, after being separated from those he sang for and then learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, he no longer plays or sings at all; when Khan Saheb asks after the instrument, Basanta Ray says the sitar is still there but "only its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned"—an image of his own broken, unstrung heart. Just as the untunable sitar can produce no music, Basanta Ray, emptied of the joy that came from his beloved, can no longer create or find pleasure in his art, his silence and abandoned instrument expressing his deepening despair over Udayaditya's fate.

Before, Udayaditya was known for his courage—he would fight against oppression with all his might and, without considering the consequences, would stop officials from abusing subjects and protect them. After Surma's death, however, a blind fear of Pratapaditya took hold of him: his former courage was gone, and he no longer intervened. When he heard of club-wielding men being sent to loot and burn the Chhapra zamindar's estate, he prepared to go but then turned back and sent his horse away. When he saw a royal official beating a tied, crying subject, he fled into his house instead of stopping the beating as he once would have. He also lost the courage to help Bhagavat and Sitaram financially, repeatedly hesitating until the money was never sent. In short, he changed from a bold defender of the oppressed into a hesitant, fear-paralyzed man who withdrew from intervening on their behalf.

Sitaram frees Udayaditya from prison: he sets (or makes use of) a fire in the palace to create chaos, enters Udayaditya's dark cell, and leads him out into the open field, helping him escape — thereby undoing the imprisonment that had resulted from their forged-petition conspiracy.

On the first occasion, Rammohan extracted Ramchandra Ray from the palace of Jessore by going up to the palace roof, tying several thick sheets together into a huge rope fastened to a pillar, lifting Ramchandra onto his back, climbing down the rope to just above the waiting boat in the canal, then letting go with his hands to grip the rope with his teeth, releasing Ramchandra from his back and lowering him carefully into the boat before jumping down himself.

On the second occasion, after the king (Ramchandra) had rejected and cruelly insulted Vibha, causing her to faint, Rammohan lifted the unconscious, exhausted Vibha and carried her out of the palace, placing her into one of the palanquins waiting near the gate.

When preparing to receive Ramchandra Ray in Jessore, Vibha is dressed elaborately as a royal princess by the Mahishi—adorned with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and carefully styled hair—bearing "the burden of her coiffure, her nose ring, her arms full of bangles," radiant with shy joy. But when she finally seeks him out in Chandradwip, she rejects a palanquin, declaring she is no queen but will go "like a common subject, like a beggar-woman." Dressed plainly as a common woman, she enters the palace "like any other maidservant," unadorned and humbled—so unrecognizable that the king mistakes her for a "beggar woman... come seeking alms." Thus she shifts from being lavishly jeweled and styled as an honored royal bride to appearing as a bare, humble, beggar-like commoner.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death, the window is a site of grief, memory, and futile longing: Udayaditya sits there gazing at the familiar moonlight, garden, and breeze, hoping against hope that Surma will return to the seat she used to occupy, only to find it empty. The window holds the ghost of the lost beloved and his despair at her absence.

In the prison cell, the window transforms into a symbol of hope and freedom: through its small frame he sees the sliver of sky, the birds flying, the bamboo grove, and the Shiva temple. Looking at the sky and birds, he believes his cage will one day break and he will be liberated, "swim in that endless sky." He explains that if he moves away from the window he sees only darkness and forgets he will ever be free—so the window now sustains his faith in eventual release, whereas the bedchamber window once only deepened his sorrow.

The relationship begins as a flirtatious financial arrangement: Rukmini (Mangala), a beautiful widow who lends money at interest, lends to the penniless but stylish palace guard Sitaram, who is drawn to both her beauty and her silver. They exchange playful endearments (Pran, Priye, Priyatame, Pranpriye) and witty banter, though Sitaram never repays his loans and keeps visiting. They later confer in secret about a scheme requiring Bhagavat's help.

The dynamic sours when Udayaditya is imprisoned: Sitaram storms into Rukmini's house, curses her, all but strikes her, and threatens to burn her home down and deface her. Rukmini, enraged and jealous (insisting the Yubaraj is *her* Yubaraj), is left seething with hatred.

It becomes life-threatening after Sitaram engineers Udayaditya's escape—setting fires to the palace and prison cell and faking the Yubaraj's death. Planning to flee Jessore, he decides to rob Rukmini's house (believing she is dead). Entering the dark cottage, he finds her in a ghastly, ghost-like state—wet clothes, disheveled hair, ashen face, trembling violently—having "returned from the door of Yama" (having nearly died). Consumed by rage, Rukmini declares she will "lay you and the Yubaraj in the oven," and goes to the next room to fetch a curved blade to kill him. Sitaram, realizing the threat is real (his own earlier metaphorical willingness to die twisting into genuine terror), slips out and flees. Recognizing that Mangala now knows everything about the escape and could expose him, he decides to flee Jessore with his family that very night.

Sitaram's scheme progressed in stages:

1. **As a distraction:** He first set fire to the guards' living huts near the prison, where their cots, utensils, clothes, and belongings were kept. This sent every guard rushing off to save their property, and the guards at Udayaditya's door—under no strict watch anyway—were the first to flee. The resulting chaos ("Fire! Fire!", hundreds of voices, frantic footsteps) let Sitaram lead Udayaditya out of his cell and through the palace undetected.

2. **Escalation into a cover-up:** Once Udayaditya was safe, Sitaram turned the ruse into a deliberate fake-death. His men set fire to the Yubaraj's now-empty cell, igniting the windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, and wooden fences. Sitaram himself threw bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the burning cell. Meanwhile, his planted men among the firefighters sabotaged the effort—pouring water where there was no fire, pretending to fetch water, breaking pots, and stumbling into one another—so the blaze would rage and the prison would collapse convincingly.

3. **Spreading the false story:** Sitaram's agents then manufactured "evidence" and testimony—shouting that the Yubaraj's cell had caught fire, that his screams were heard from within, and that the roof had collapsed with no response. Sitaram intended to spread the news that the Yubaraj had died in the fire. This was later reinforced at court by witnesses who claimed to have seen Udayaditya through the window and heard his screams, plus the melted, burnt remains of his sword recovered from the cell—leading Pratapaditya to believe his brother had perished, thereby concealing the escape.

Ramchandra Ray shows no gratitude at all. The fact that Udayaditya had ignored his own danger to save his life "went up in smoke," and instead Ramchandra brings up Udayaditya's name only to mock and joke about him in his court—treating his very identity as a son of Pratapaditya as his crime. He rationalizes that such rescue was bound to happen (that everyone would surely unite to save him), and further believes Udayaditya saved him merely for the sake of his own sister rather than out of genuine concern. Being a fickle, small-minded man consumed by his own self-importance, he feels no thankfulness and readily joins the courtiers (especially Ramai Bhand) in ridiculing Udayaditya, thinking only of what others would think of him if he defended his brother-in-law.

The mechanism is a forged petition. Bhagavat and Sitaram conspire to write a fake complaint—sealed with the Yubaraj's own ring (the one Rukmini had brought)—written as though Prince Udayaditya were reporting his father's treason to the Emperor of Delhi in order to seize the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat then brings this petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted the servant who was carrying it toward Delhi and that the servant had fled the country. Thus the very imperial authority Pratapaditya had scornfully dismissed—declaring "The Emperor of Delhi is not my God" and forbidding the minister to invoke his name—becomes the instrument of the prince's condemnation: the forged appeal to the Dillishwar makes it appear that his own son has turned to the Emperor against him.

In Surma's presence, grooming Vibha's hair was an act of intimate, affectionate care that expressed their close bond: when the aged Mahishi was forcibly adorning Vibha for her husband's arrival—forcing eight thick gold bangles, a huge diamond bracelet, and an unbecoming nose ring on her—Vibha "secretly went to Surma and had her hair done to her own liking." Surma's touch represented the one personal, gentle attention that let Vibha keep a piece of herself amid the Mahishi's overwhelming adornment. (The Mahishi, however, saw the style as "flawed," attributed it to Surma's jealousy, and undid and restyled it herself.)

In Surma's tragic absence, the same act of hair-grooming becomes the clearest marker of her loss. When it is time to braid her hair, Vibha "sits quietly, as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it for her; she is waiting for her"—but evening falls, night approaches, and Surma does not come, so "her hair remains unbraided." The unbraided hair embodies the waiting that will not be answered and the comfort (Surma once came at the slightest sadness to soothe her) that is now gone. Finally, when Rammohan arrives, he notes, "Your hair is unkempt... It seems there is no one here to care for you!"—so that Vibha's neglected, unbraided hair stands as outward proof that Surma, who once tended it, is no longer there to care for her.
